title: Waves and Sound

cards.h: How a voice crosses a room
cards.b:
When you speak, nothing travels from your mouth to a friend's ear except a disturbance. The air itself only jiggles in place. The pattern of the jiggle moves on, passing the message from molecule to molecule.

That is a wave: energy travelling without matter travelling. Sound, ripples, earthquakes, radio, light and even the waves of quantum physics all share this behaviour.

Transverse waves shake the medium at right angles to the wave's direction. A rope flicked up and down, or water ripples. Light is also transverse.

Longitudinal waves push and pull along the direction of travel, creating squeezed regions (compressions) and stretched regions (rarefactions). Sound in air is longitudinal.

Sound needs a medium (air, water, steel). It cannot cross empty space, which is why space is silent.

Wave speed

v = f x wavelength

Frequency f (waves per second) times wavelength (length of one wave) gives the speed. The speed is set by the medium; the source sets the frequency. So higher frequency means shorter wavelength, at the same speed.

Pitch is frequency: a high note has high f. Humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Loudness depends on amplitude and is measured in decibels (dB): ordinary talk is about 60 dB, and sound above about 85 dB over long periods can harm hearing.

In air at 20 degrees C sound travels at about 343 m/s. It is faster in water (about 1500 m/s) and faster still in steel (over 5000 m/s).

When waves meet, they simply add. Two crests make a bigger crest (constructive); a crest meeting a trough cancels (destructive).

Two notes of slightly different frequencies, such as 440 and 444 Hz, make a throbbing sound at 4 beats per second. Musicians use this to tune instruments: when the beats vanish, the notes match. Noise-cancelling headphones use destructive interference on purpose.

cards.h: The Doppler effect and standing waves
cards.b:
When a source moves toward you, waves bunch up and the pitch rises; when it moves away, the pitch drops. Think of an ambulance siren passing. Christian Doppler predicted this in 1842.

A string fixed at both ends supports standing waves at special frequencies: the fundamental and its multiples (harmonics). Guitars, flutes and organ pipes make music from these. Radar guns and weather radar use the Doppler shift too.

Concert A is 440 Hz. In air at 343 m/s, wavelength = 343 / 440 = 0.78 m.

Thunder: light reaches you almost instantly, sound takes time. If you hear thunder 3 s after the flash, the lightning is about 343 x 3 = 1030 m, roughly 1 km away. Each 3 seconds of delay is about one kilometre.

An echo returning from a wall after 0.2 s means the wall is 343 x 0.2 / 2 = 34 m away (half, since the sound goes there and back).

• 'Sound travels faster when louder.' Speed depends on the medium, not loudness or pitch.
  • 'Sound is fastest in air because air is light.' It is faster in denser, stiffer media like steel.
  • 'The wave carries the water or air along.' The particles only oscillate; the energy moves on.

cards.h: Doppler radar and the Indian ear
cards.b:
The India Meteorological Department uses Doppler weather radars to track the winds inside cyclones by the shift in frequency of reflected waves. This gives hours of warning before landfall.

Indian classical music builds on exact frequency ratios and resonance. C. V. Raman's work on the harmonics of the tabla and mridangam showed why their sound is so musical. The Indian Navy and fishermen also use sonar, sound pulses and echoes, to find objects under water.

• Waves carry energy, not matter. They are transverse or longitudinal.
  • v = f x wavelength.
  • Sound in air travels at about 343 m/s; it needs a medium.
  • Waves interfere; the Doppler effect shifts frequency for moving sources.

Think about it

1. Why does your voice sound deeper to you when you speak than on a recording?
2. If you shout in a canyon and hear the echo after 4 s, how wide is the canyon?
